title: quest instructions task-execution says checkbox edits are index-addressed; the flags take the 1-based position, and quest help task edit already says so
description:
Reported by opum-doc 2026-09-15 against quest 0.7.1, verified here.

`quest instructions task-execution` said, verbatim: "Checkbox edits are index-addressed, so two editors do not overwrite each other: `--check-ac 2`, `--uncheck-dod 1`, `--remove-ac 3`."

The flags take the 1-based `position`, not the 0-based `index`. Measured on a three-criterion task:
  --check-ac 0   exit 2, "--check-ac must be a 1-based positive integer."
  --check-ac 1   exit 0, checks index 0 / position 1
  --check-ac 3   exit 0, checks index 2 / position 3
  --check-ac 4   exit 6, out of range

THE SHARPER FRAMING, which is not the one reported. This is not "docs versus behaviour" generally. `quest help task edit` ALREADY says it correctly and at length: "Checklist positions are 1-based and reader-facing ... address an item by the `position` field ... Each entry also keeps its 0-based `index` for programmatic addressing (position is always index + 1); `index` is not what these flags take." So TWO DOCUMENTATION SURFACES OF THE SAME CLI CONTRADICTED EACH OTHER, and the wrong one is the surface the agent protocol sends a caller to first -- this repository's own CLAUDE.md instructs reading `quest instructions task-execution` before task lifecycle actions. A caller who follows the protocol gets the wrong answer; one who runs `help` gets the right one.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN A TYPO, opum-doc's analysis and it holds: the failure is quiet in the direction that matters. A caller looping 0..4 -- the natural loop when the field is called an index and `task view` prints a 0-based `index` right beside the position -- gets ONE error on i=0 and four silent successes that check positions 1-4, leaving the LAST criterion unchecked. They caught it only by counting `checked: true` against the criterion count before closing, and a session trusting the per-call exit codes would close a task with an unchecked criterion under a final summary claiming all of them met.

ONE REFINEMENT TO THE REPORT, measured rather than assumed. They wrote that the error "names the argument you passed rather than the off-by-one" and proposed a message stating the 1-based base. That message already exists: 0.7.1 returns "--check-ac must be a 1-based positive integer." So the suggested fix was already shipped, and their loop did receive the base in the one error it got. The usability point survives -- one legible error among four silent wrong successes is still easy to read as a single bad call -- but the CLI is not silent about the base, and the record should not say it was.

WHY NOTHING CAUGHT IT. QCLI-148's guide test executes every command a guide shows, and `--check-ac 2` executes fine. Only the word describing it was wrong. A command that EXECUTES and a sentence that DESCRIBES it correctly are different objects, and only the first was under test.

acceptanceCriteria.text: quest instructions task-execution describes checkbox edits by the 1-based position, names the 0-based index as NOT what the flags take, and agrees with quest help task edit rather than contradicting it

A test ties the guide's prose to MEASURED behaviour -- it checks position 1, reads the record back to confirm index 0 was the item affected, and confirms the 0-based spelling is refused -- rather than asserting a wording against another wording
The gate is proven both ways as two runs: red against the original 'index-addressed' text, green against the corrected text

implementationNotes:
THIS IS A RESIDUAL OF QCLI-269, NOT A NEW DEFECT -- found by following an unmerged branch name (fix/QCLI-269-check-ac-position-mismatch) that surfaced while measuring something unrelated. It changes what the gate has to be.

QCLI-269 (Done, 2026-09-13, PR #50, 26f8d9f) fixed EXACTLY this defect: it added the presentation-only 1-based `position` field to every checklist entry, corrected src/application/command-help.ts, and corrected the guide prose. Read from the diff rather than the commit message: the guide it corrected is TASK-CREATION, whose "Checklist positions renumber after a removal" section now reads "address ... by its 1-based `position` field (QCLI-269) ... `index` is not what these flags take".

TASK-EXECUTION says the same thing about the same flags, twelve lines of prose away in the same file, and was left saying "index-addressed". Two guides, one fixed, one missed, in a single commit that touched ten files and was otherwise thorough -- including a two-pass consumer sweep across five repositories.

SO THE GATE CANNOT NAME A GUIDE. My first version asserted on task-execution specifically, which would have repeated the original mistake the moment a fourth surface appeared. It now iterates EVERY guide: none may contain "index-addressed", and every guide that both shows `--check-ac` and talks about addressing must say "1-based" and "position". A guide that merely shows `--check-ac 1` in a recipe makes no claim about addressing and is not required to explain it -- that distinction is deliberate, because a gate that demands an explanation wherever the flag appears pushes the next author to paste boilerplate into task-finalization's recipe rather than write anything true.

Measured: three guides mention `--check-ac`; two of them explain addressing; task-finalization shows it in a recipe without claiming anything about it.

PROOF, both directions:
  clean tree                                          green
  revert ONLY task-execution to "index-addressed"     RED
  -- that is the exact state QCLI-269 left behind, so the gate is proven
     against the real historical defect rather than against a synthetic one
  restored                                            green

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THE FIX. "A fix applied at the site where a defect was reported is the easiest kind to under-apply" was written into QCLI-314's notes earlier tonight, from a CI guard where the same diagnosis had to be applied at three sites and I applied it at one. Here is the same failure, by a different author, two days earlier, inside this repository's own tracker history, on a defect about the tracker's own docs. That is three independent instances in one repository, which makes it a property of how fixes get scoped and not a run of bad luck.

The transferable form: WHEN A FIX CORRECTS A CLAIM, ENUMERATE EVERY PLACE THAT CLAIM IS MADE AND GATE THE ENUMERATION, not the instances. QCLI-269 corrected two of three surfaces and shipped a test for the behaviour; nothing asserted the set of surfaces was complete, so the third was invisible to it.

TWO REFINEMENTS TO THE ENUMERATION RULE, from opum-doc applying it within the hour on a different repository and a different claim (ODOC-216, itself a residual of ODOC-211 one hour apart -- the same relationship this task has to QCLI-269 two days apart).

1. "ENUMERATE EVERY PLACE THE CLAIM IS MADE" READS AS BEING ABOUT SOURCE FILES, AND IN THEIR CASE ZERO OF THE PLACES WERE. Handed three corrections, they grepped before patching. Two claims were confined to the single file they had been pointed at -- the boring outcome, and worth having because confined-by-measurement and confined-by-assumption are different facts and only one is reportable. The third claim was NOT IN THE NAMED FILE AT ALL: zero hits across scripts/, .github/ and docs/, because it lived in a completed task's implementation notes, its final summary, and a merged PR body. A session patching the three instances it was handed would have shipped a clean file under records still making the false claim.

So the rule has at least three media tonight: code/code (this task -- two guide files, one fixed, one missed), code/records (theirs -- the fix belonged in neither the file nor the record it was filed against), and the CI-guard case in QCLI-314 (one diagnosis, three call sites). The word "place" has to mean any surface that asserts the claim, including tracker records and PR bodies, which are exactly the surfaces a code-shaped grep does not reach.

2. PREFER MAKING A CLAIM MEASURED OVER MAKING IT CORRECT. Enumeration found their surfaces; it did not tell them what to do about a claim sitting in a completed task and a merged PR body, neither of which should be rewritten. They fixed it FORWARD: the suite now prints `environment: bash <version>, git <version>` above its verdict, so the claim is measured on every future run, plus a correcting note where the wrong sentence lives. Their formulation is the one to keep -- a retraction makes the record honest; making the thing measurable means the next reader does not need the record to be honest, and only the second survives the next author.

That applies directly to this task's own gate and is the better justification for its shape than the one recorded above. The gate does not assert that the guides are correct; it asserts a property that is re-measured on every run against the live guide set, so a guide added next year is covered by a check nobody has to remember to extend. Asserting correctness would have aged; asserting the enumeration does not.
